title: Fixed-Target Dirichlet Selection and a Sharp Obstruction at n = 3

meta.author: Lean Genius
originalContributions: legendreSym_eq_of_prime_modeq: periodicity of the Legendre symbol in the prime — the load-bearing fact the parent slice oq-03-oq-07 only asserted in prose. For odd primes p, q with p ≡ q (mod 4·|a|), legendreSym p a = legendreSym q a. Mathlib packages jacobiSym.mod_right (J(a|b) depends on the modulus b only mod 4|a|) but not its Legendre-symbol-in-the-prime counterpart; the proof bridges the two via legendreSym.to_jacobiSym. Specialised to a = −n (qr_condition_class_invariant) this is exactly the statement that the geometry's QR hypothesis legendreSym p (−n) = 1 depends only on the residue class p mod 4n, making the Dirichlet selection a genuine fixed-target problem.

exists_qr_qualified_multiplier_prime / exists_qr_qualified_multiplier_prime_full: the conditional reduction of oq-03-oq-07 upgraded to an unconditional supply. Given a single residue r with gcd(r,4n)=1, r ≡ −1 (mod n) and J(−n | r) = 1, Dirichlet's theorem (Nat.forall_exists_prime_gt_and_modEq, modulus 4n) supplies for every bound N a prime p > N with p ≡ r (mod 4n); by periodicity legendreSym p (−n) = J(−n | r) = 1 holds outright, and p ≡ −1 (mod n) gives the multiplier shape p = d·n − 1. Routed through the parent reduction this also forces the geometry's hypothesis legendreSym p (−d) = 1 — the QR side condition is now produced, not merely reduced. Witnessed non-vacuous at n = 2, r = 3 (qr_qualified_multiplier_prime_two).

legendreSym_neg_three_eq_neg_one / multiplier_prime_neg_three_qr_fails / multiplier_route_incomplete_at_three: a sharp negative result. Every multiplier prime for n = 3 satisfies p ≡ −1 ≡ 2 (mod 3), and for every such odd prime legendreSym p (−3) = −1 (the value is forced onto p mod 12 ∈ {5,11}, where J(−3 | ·) = −1). Hence the geometry's QR hypothesis legendreSym p (−n) = 1 is satisfiable by NO multiplier prime for n = 3, even though 3 = 1² + 1² + 1² is plainly a sum of three squares. Equivalently the qualifying-residue hypothesis of the positive result fails at n = 3. This documents, concretely and rigorously, why the multiplier–QR route of oq-03-oq-07 is only established for the small multipliers d ∈ {1,2}: the naive −n-residue condition cannot on its own certify representability; a qualifying class exists iff n avoids Legendre's excluded form 4^a(8b+7), so the existence of r is exactly the genus condition.

Nat.forall_exists_prime_gt_and_modEq (Mathlib, NumberTheory/LSeries/PrimesInAP): Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions; here used with modulus 4n to select primes p ≡ r (mod 4n) in the qualifying residue class.

Proofs.LagrangeFourSquaresWaringG2OQ03OQ07.legendreSym_neg_n_one_imp_neg_d_one (parent slice, 0-axiom): the multiplier reduction legendreSym p (−n) = 1 ⟹ legendreSym p (−d) = 1 that the unconditional supply feeds into to force the geometry's hypothesis on d.

conclusion.summary: A follow-up to the multiplier–quadratic-residue reduction (oq-03-oq-07) that does three things, all 0-axiom. (1) Periodicity: it proves the parent's prose-only claim that the QR condition legendreSym p (−n) = 1 is a property of the residue class p mod 4n — for odd primes p ≡ q (mod 4n), legendreSym p (−n) = legendreSym q (−n) — via Mathlib's jacobiSym.mod_right through legendreSym.to_jacobiSym, a Legendre-symbol-in-the-prime statement Mathlib does not package. (2) Unconditional supply: given a single residue r with gcd(r,4n)=1, r ≡ −1 (mod n) and J(−n | r) = 1, Dirichlet's theorem (modulus 4n) yields arbitrarily large multiplier primes p = d·n − 1 for which legendreSym p (−n) = 1 — and hence, through the parent reduction, legendreSym p (−d) = 1 — hold outright; the parent's conditional reduction becomes an unconditional supply, witnessed non-vacuous at n = 2, r = 3. (3) A sharp obstruction: for n = 3 every multiplier prime has p ≡ 2 (mod 3) and legendreSym p (−3) = −1, so no multiplier prime satisfies the geometry's QR hypothesis even though 3 = 1²+1²+1²; equivalently no qualifying residue class exists at n = 3. 244 lines, 10 theorems, 0 definitions, 0 axioms, 0 sorries; verified to depend only on propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound.
conclusion.implications: The periodicity theorem closes the precise gap the parent left open in prose, confirming that selecting a multiplier prime is a fixed-target Dirichlet problem. The positive supply theorem isolates the entire residual difficulty into one statement — the existence of a qualifying residue class r — and discharges everything around it unconditionally. The n = 3 obstruction makes the cost of that isolation explicit and honest: a qualifying class need not exist, and in fact exists iff n avoids Legendre's excluded form 4^a(8b+7), so 'there is a qualifying r' is equivalent to the genus condition itself — the genuine open content of the parent umbrella, here exhibited concretely failing at n = 3. Together they sharpen the record of exactly what the −n-multiplier route can and cannot do, and explain why oq-03-oq-07's geometry is established only for the small multipliers d ∈ {1,2}.

openQuestions.question: Characterise exactly the n for which a qualifying residue class r (with gcd(r,4n)=1, r ≡ −1 (mod n) and J(−n | r) = 1) exists, and prove it coincides with the non-excluded classes n ≠ 4^a(8b+7). The n = 3 obstruction proved here is the first instance of non-existence; a full characterisation would, combined with exists_qr_qualified_multiplier_prime_full, reduce three-square sufficiency on the qualifying classes entirely to the d ∈ {1,2} geometry — i.e. settle the selection layer completely. Likely route: analyse J(−n | ·) as a real Dirichlet character mod 4n restricted to the coset p ≡ −1 (mod n), and show it is non-constant (takes value +1) precisely off the excluded form.

Generalise the n = 3 obstruction to a uniform family: identify all n (e.g. a congruence/genus description) for which legendreSym p (−n) = −1 for every prime p ≡ −1 (mod n), and prove the corresponding multiplier_route_incomplete statement once for the whole family rather than the single value n = 3.
